title: Spec: Data management and startup recovery
description:
# Spec: Data management and startup recovery

## Problem Statement

A TuxBooks user cannot see where the app stores its data or how much space it uses. The data lives in two OS locations the user never chose, and the app never shows them. There is no supported way to clear data the app regenerates on its own if it grows or misbehaves.

When the app fails to start, it fails silently. A corrupt or unreadable database makes the sidecar exit, and the main process calls `app.quit()` with only a stderr line. A user who launches from the desktop sees no window and no message, with no path forward.

The user is also wary of any reset feature. They cannot tell which files belong to the app and which are their books, so they fear deleting the wrong directory or their library.

## Solution

A Data tab in Settings that shows every app-owned location with its resolved path and size, lists the watched book folders with book counts and file sizes, and keeps the user's books visually and conceptually separate from app data. A cache clear removes only the data the app regenerates by itself, behind a plain confirmation.

Startup recovery adds a durable error log in the app data directory, a native dialog naming the failure and offering to open the data folder, and self-healing that quarantines a broken database instead of deleting it and then starts fresh. A `--reset-data` flag and a `--dry-run` companion cover the command-line and shell-launched cases.

## User Stories

1. As a TuxBooks user, I want to see every folder the app stores data in, so that I know what is on my disk.
2. As a user, I want to see how much space each app data item uses, so that I can decide whether to clear anything.
3. As a user, I want the app's own data shown separately from my book files, so that I never mistake one for the other.
4. As a user, I want to see the folders I have added as libraries, with the number of books under each, so that I can confirm what is indexed.
5. As a user, I want to see the total size of the book files under each watched folder, so that I understand my library footprint.
6. As a user, I want to open any data folder in my file manager, so that I can inspect it myself.
7. As a user, I want to copy any data path, so that I can use it elsewhere.
8. As a user, I want each data row labeled as derived or as the only copy, so that I know what is safe to clear.
9. As a user, I want to clear the caches the app rebuilds on its own, so that I can recover space or reset browser state without risk.
10. As a user, I want a confirmation before clearing that names what goes and what stays, so that I am not surprised.
11. As a user, I want to see how much a clear freed, so that I know it worked.
12. As a user, I want the reassurance, stated plainly, that clearing app data never removes my books, so that I trust the feature.
13. As a user, I want to see the counts of my catalog (books, authors, collections, annotations, and reading progress), so that I understand what the database holds.
14. As a user, I want to see that my theme and reader settings are app data, so that I know a full reset would affect them.
15. As a user, I want the app to write a startup error log, so that a failure leaves a trace I can share.
16. As a user, I want a clear dialog when the app cannot start, telling me what failed and where the log is, so that I am not left guessing.
17. As a user, I want one button in that dialog to open the data folder, so that I can act on the message.
18. As a user, I want the app to keep a broken database instead of deleting it, so that nothing is lost and a bug can be diagnosed.
19. As a user, I want the app to start with a fresh database after quarantining a broken one, so that I get a working app back.
20. As a user, I want to be told where the quarantined file went, so that I can recover or delete it later.
21. As a user, I want a `--reset-data` command, so that I can recover from a terminal when the app will not start.
22. As a user, I want `--reset-data` to quarantine rather than delete, so that recovery is reversible, and the quarantined file is left in place for me to remove myself.
23. As a user, I want a `--dry-run` that prints the paths and sizes without touching anything, so that I can see the blast radius first.
24. As a user, I want the terminal message to include a copy-paste command, so that recovery does not require reading docs.
25. As a user, I want the exact resolved paths printed, not a guess, so that they match my machine.
26. As a user, I want clearing cache to leave my theme and reader settings alone, so that my preferences survive.
27. As a user, I want clearing cache to leave my catalog and reading progress alone, so that nothing important is lost.
28. As a user, I want a note that some browser cache rebuilds while the app runs, so that the numbers make sense.
29. As a maintainer, I want App data and Cache defined in the glossary, so that the boundary is not re-litigated.
30. As a maintainer, I want the recovery rules recorded as an ADR, so that the quarantine choice and the books-are-never-touched rule have a home.

## Implementation Decisions

- Glossary. Add App data and Cache to CONTEXT.md. App data is everything TuxBooks stores to run: the catalog database, the cover cache, the GPU fallback marker, and the browser caches and settings in the Electron config directory. It never includes the user's book files. Cache is the subset of app data the app regenerates by itself: the Chromium browser caches and the GPU fallback marker. The catalog, the cover cache, and the settings sit outside it.
- ADR. Record two rules: a broken database is quarantined, never deleted, and the reset paths never touch book files or watched locations.
- Two app-owned roots. The data root holds the catalog database with its WAL and shared memory files, the cover cache, and the GPU fallback marker. The Electron config root holds the browser caches and the localStorage settings. The config path is read at runtime, never hardcoded, because the packaged directory name is uncertain.
- Storage report read model. One structure returns the data root entries, the config root entries, the cache total, the watched book locations, the total book bytes, and the catalog counts. Each entry carries a stable id, a friendly label, a resolved path, a size in bytes, and a kind of derived, only-copy, or settings.
- Per-location book stats come from a new sidecar aggregate query that groups books by the watched location whose path prefixes them, summing file size and counting rows. The schema already stores each book's size, so no migration is needed.
- Cache clear is a main-process action. It removes only the browser cache directories under the config root and the GPU fallback marker. It leaves the catalog, the cover cache, the settings, and book files untouched, and it returns the bytes freed.
- The cover cache is inspectable but not clearable from the cache action. Covers are extracted at import and read from disk, nothing re-extracts a missing cover, and a rescan skips unchanged books, so clearing covers while the catalog references them would strip cover art until the book changes. A full `--reset-data` may remove it: the reset quarantines the catalog first, so the covers are unreferenced, and the startup sweep (`sweep_unreferenced_covers`) removes unreferenced covers on the next launch anyway. A rebuild path is out of scope.
- Settings to main is a new boundary. The Data tab needs a read call and an act call the current sidecar invoke channel does not provide. Add two explicit channels, a storage report read and a cache clear, with the same sender gate as the existing channels, plus the preload methods and typed bridge wrappers. Add a main-process action to open an app data folder that resolves the path from an id on the main side.
- The renderer never names a filesystem path for these actions. Rows carry stable ids and main resolves the real path.
- Startup error log. On any fatal startup failure, main writes a timestamped line to a startup error log in the data root, naming the failure and the resolved data and config paths.
- Startup error dialog. On a fatal failure, main shows a native error dialog with a plain sentence, the log path, and one button that opens the data root.
- Startup quarantine. When the database cannot be opened, an integrity check fails, or migrations fail, the sidecar moves the database and its WAL and shared memory files aside under a timestamped quarantine name, then initializes a fresh database and reports what it did. It never deletes the broken files.
- Startup flags. `--reset-data` clears app data and never books, and quarantines the database. `--dry-run` prints the resolved paths and sizes and exits without changes. The flags are parsed before app ready, ahead of the single-instance lock.
- Terminal message. The same fatal failure prints to stderr with the resolved paths and a copy-paste command.
- The existing GPU fallback marker is the precedent for next-launch self-healing and stays as it is.

## Testing Decisions

- Good tests assert external behavior: what the report contains, what a clear removes and reports, what a corrupt database leads to, and what the UI shows. They do not assert internal function names or call order.
- Main IPC handlers, tested through the injected-dependency registrar with a fake sidecar, dialog, and shell. Prior art `frontend/tests/security/ipcHandlers.test.ts`. Covers the report shape, the cache clear removing only cache entries and returning freed bytes, the open-folder action resolving a path by id and never accepting a renderer path, and the sender gate on the new channels.
- Security boundary, tested in `frontend/tests/security/pathSchema.test.ts` for any new parser or channel constant, with a `just test-e2e-security` run because the IPC and policy surface changes.
- Sidecar, tested with Rust unit tests at the repository and command layer for the per-location aggregate query, prior art `library_locations.rs` and `artwork_cache.rs`, and an integration test for quarantine that points the database path at a corrupt file, initializes, and asserts a quarantined copy exists and a working database replaced it.
- Frontend Data tab, tested with the `mockInvoke` bridge mock. Prior art `frontend/tests/SettingsShell.test.tsx`. Covers the two roots and their sizes rendering, book locations rendering with counts, the reassurance line, the clear button opening a confirmation that names what goes and stays, and clearing updating the displayed sizes.
- The new boot-recovery module, tested as pure functions with injected fs and dialog for flag parsing, the log line content, the dialog decision, and the dry-run path that changes nothing.

## Out of Scope

- A full app data wipe UI.
- Clearing or rebuilding the cover cache while the catalog still references it. A full reset may remove it, since it quarantines the catalog first and the covers are then unreferenced.
- Removing a watched library location.
- Database compaction, a rescan button, and a last-scanned timestamp.
- Windows and macOS packaging behavior.
- An in-app safe mode.

## Further Notes

- The data root and config root are each resolved in two places today, main and sidecar. Keep the resolutions consistent; a single source of truth for the data path is a possible follow-up.
- The books-are-never-touched rule already holds in the code: removing a book deletes only the database row, and import indexes in place. This spec extends that rule to the recovery paths.

comments.author: Tuomo Tuunanen
comments.text: Resolutions after review. 1) Covers and reset: the not-clearable rule applies to the cache-clear action while books remain; a full --reset-data may remove the cover cache, because it quarantines the catalog first and the startup sweep removes the unreferenced covers on the next launch anyway. 2) --reset-data always quarantines the database; the 'by default' wording implied a delete option we are not adding. 3) The config-root Settings row is relabeled 'Settings and other app files', since settings are loose files with no single path.

title: Restore full Smart Dark by extending the PDFium forks (object-level recolor, scans, shadings)
description:
Context. Moving the PDF engine to PDFium forced Smart Dark to be simplified, and the result is coarser than what we shipped before. ADR 0002 records it: 'Smart Dark loses object-level recoloring and scanned-image classification. FPDF_COLORSCHEME recolors by category ... This is an accepted degradation.' docs/PDF.md spells out the cost: all path fills share one colour, images are not a colour-scheme category so photographs, covers, screenshots and scans keep their pixels, scanned-image classification is out of scope, FPDF_CONVERT_FILL_TO_STROKE is a workaround so adjacent fills stay legible, and a page that is one large image is left as-is. tuxbooks-koe.9 dropped object recoloring and scan classification on purpose, and the epic's user story 16 called the coarser recolor acceptable only for the first version.

How we got here. The old MuPDF Smart Dark was an object-level recolor device (issue #67, PR #79) and it is where MuPDF's heap corruption lived: the JS device binding handed native references to JS callbacks and expected JS GC to release them, so the reader grew guardrails (worker recycling every 180 Smart Dark renders and SMART_RENDER_RECYCLE_LIMIT; a transformed-image cache that destroyed its own entries, PR #99; borrowed-shading drop, PR #117; the leak and recycle fix, PR #98). PDFium's public API has no per-object device hook and no image category, only the four FPDF_COLORSCHEME categories, so the object-level device was deleted with the engine. Note that the failure class, not object-level recoloring itself, was the reason for the guardrails.

Why this can be revisited. We now own forks of the renderer: tuxbooks/runtime (fork of embedpdf/runtime) and tuxbooks/pdfium (fork of chromium/pdfium), see tuxbooks-nkf. PDFium is C++ in wasm with no JS callback handing native references across the GC boundary, so an object-level or image-aware color transform implemented inside the fork should not carry the MuPDF defect class. The simplification was forced by the public API surface, not because object-level recoloring is unstable in principle.

What to build in the fork, options to decide:
1. Image-aware recoloring: adjust or invert photographs, screenshots and covers instead of the current all-images-untouched rule.
2. Scanned-image classification: detect a paper-backed scan (one large image, light background) and remap its pixels, matching the retired behavior.
3. Hue-preserving vector fills: recolor colored path fills with a transform that keeps hue relationships instead of collapsing every fill to one colour.
4. Shading handling: render shadings under the scheme, closing the borrowed-shading problem from PR #117.
5. A per-object color hook in PDFium exposed through the wasm binding and the @embedpdf loader, so the palette lives in TuxBooks and the engine stays general.

Then wire it: build the wasm from the fork using the toolchain in tuxbooks-nkf, point TuxBooks at it, extend smartColors.ts and the worker render request, and keep the smart/original cache variant key.

Acceptance, to refine after a decision:
- A concrete Smart Dark spec agreed first: what photographs, screenshots, scans, colored vector fills and shadings should look like, benchmarked against Papers' dark modes where they apply.
- Implemented in tuxbooks/runtime, and in tuxbooks/pdfium if the change belongs upstream, built reproducibly and consumed by TuxBooks.
- No WASM heap growth and no worker recycling under the zoom churn E2E, so the old guardrail class does not return.
- Real-WASM dark render tests for the image, scan, colored fill and shading cases, plus a seeded E2E dark-mode assertion.
acceptance_criteria: Decide the full Smart Dark behaviour and where it lives (TuxBooks palette plus an engine hook, or in the fork). If pursued, ship a reproducibly built fork wasm that TuxBooks consumes, restore the desired image, scan, colored-fill and shading behaviour, and prove no heap or worker-recycling regression with the churn E2E.

comments.author: Tuomo Tuunanen
comments.text:
Fixed on branch fix/scale-swap-test-flake, commit 88c5fa6, PR #132
(https://github.com/tuunanet/tuxbooks/pull/132).

What made it flaky: the test called doc.releaseRender(n) as soon as the
canvas mounted, but the fake registers the held page.render promise a beat
later, after the canvas effect's first await. When the release won that race
it hit an empty table and the held render never resolved, so
waitFor(data-render-state="rendered") timed out. Coverage instrumentation
widens the window. This is a test-double race, not a reader bug.

Deterministic wait: no wall-clock wait remains. The fake now queues a release
that arrives before its held render and resolves the render as soon as it
registers (frontend/tests/mocks/pdfEngine.ts). The test waits only on the
reader's own data-render-state and data-pdf-render-quality attributes.

Stronger assertion: after the zoom every previously rendered canvas must
report data-pdf-render-quality="scaled", which is the no-blank proof because
the held render cannot be final yet. Releasing the two budgeted pages must
then swap them to "final", while page 3, outside the render budget, stays
"scaled".

Runs:
- Before: the first full-file coverage run failed in setup at
  PdfReader.test.tsx:2033 (waitFor timeout); isolated target under coverage
  failed 1 in 12 runs.
- After: full file under coverage 8/8 runs report Tests 73 passed (73);
  isolated target under coverage 20/20 runs pass.
- pnpm --filter frontend exec vitest run tests/PdfReader.test.tsx: 73 passed.
- pnpm --filter frontend exec vitest run tests/PdfPageCanvas.test.tsx: 3 passed.
- just check: OK.

Note: the coverage command exits non-zero on the per-glob coverage floors when
run against a single file because the rest of the suite is not measured. The
pass/fail signal is the Tests summary.

No blockers.

title: Make Ctrl+wheel zoom smooth in the PDF reader
description:
Ctrl+wheel zoom in the PDF reader jumps. One notch snaps the zoom onto the next preset, so at 100% it goes to 125% and at 200% it goes to 400%. Each step also clears every rendered bitmap and redraws at once, so the page goes blank and sharp again while the wheel is still turning.

This ticket replaces preset stepping with a continuous zoom and defers the expensive redraw until the wheel settles. The result should feel like Okular, pdf.js, and Evince.
design:
Zoom math (new pure function in frontend/src/components/reader/pdf/pdfLayout.ts, beside stepZoomLevel and clampZoom):
wheelZoomScale(scale, deltaY, deltaMode) = clampZoom(scale * 1.2 ** (normalizedDelta / 100)), where normalizedDelta reuses the wheelScale normalization in useAxisLockedWheel.ts (deltaMode 1 is lines, deltaMode 2 is pages) and is then clamped to +/-300.

Reference points from mature readers: Okular uses zoomFactor * (1 + delta/500) with delta +/-120 per notch, about 1.24x; pdf.js uses 1.1x per tick; Evince 1.2x; zathura 1.1x. We chose 1.2x per 100px Chromium notch.

Gesture preview: while Ctrl+wheel events arrive, keep the committed layout scale and apply transform: scale(previewScale / committedScale) with transform-origin at the cursor on the pdf-document element. Canvases, text layer, and highlight overlays sit inside that element, so they scale with it and nothing re-renders. This follows pdf.js (pdf_viewer.js postpones drawing and CSS-transforms the canvas).

Settle: a 250ms trailing timeout after the last wheel event commits the preview scale. Commit updates zoom state, adjusts scrollLeft and scrollTop so the cursor point stays fixed, clears renderedPages and the bitmap cache, then renders. pdf.js uses 400ms; Okular uses gesture end. Any non-wheel zoom action flushes immediately, and unmount flushes rather than discards.

State: add a transient preview scale alongside ZoomState in PdfReader.tsx. Fit modes keep deriving their scale; the first wheel tick multiplies that derived scale and switches mode to custom.
acceptance_criteria:
- Ctrl+wheel multiplies the current zoom by 1.2 per standard 100px notch (deltaMode 0), and by the same exponential formula for smaller trackpad deltas. deltaMode 1 and 2 are normalized first.
- One wheel event is capped at 300px of delta (three notches). Zoom clamps to the existing 12% and 10000% bounds.
- The first tick out of any fit mode multiplies the actual fit scale, with no rounding onto a preset.
- During the gesture the page scales with a CSS transform and no canvas re-renders. The sharp redraw runs 250ms after the last wheel event.
- Toolbar zoom buttons, Ctrl+plus, Ctrl+minus, Ctrl+0, presets, typed zoom, fit modes, and entering or leaving presentation render immediately and cancel any pending wheel redraw.
- The toolbar zoom percentage updates live during the gesture.
- Closing the reader mid gesture commits the last zoom instead of discarding it.
- Keyboard plus and minus keep selecting the closest next preset from ZOOM_PRESETS.
- The point under the cursor stays fixed while wheel zooming, matching Okular and browsers.
- frontend/tests/PdfReader.test.tsx:1820 is rewritten for the new behavior.
- New unit tests cover the pure zoom function, a new end to end test covers Ctrl+wheel, and the reader benchmark measures wheel settle time.
notes: Touches PdfReader.tsx (zoom handler at lines 96-101 and 984-1077), pdfLayout.ts, PdfDocumentView.tsx (the transform), and PdfPageCanvas.tsx. PDF only; the EPUB reader is untouched. Related work: issue #65 (zoom mode and presets) and #68 (toolbar docking).

title: Explore forking PDFium into the tuxbooks org to fix renderer bugs ourselves
description:
Context. tuxbooks-i2a is a PDFium tiling-pattern leak: on dphi_GRANIITTI_MC.pdf the gray hatched error bands bleed roughly half a line width past their fill path. poppler (GNOME Papers/Okular) and ghostscript both clip correctly, PDFium draws about 700 stray pixels at 614 dpi. No FPDF_RENDER_* flag changes it, the clipped matrix render path leaks identically, and @embedpdf/pdfium 2.15.1 behaves like 2.15.0. This is the residual gray flecking still visible at 426.5% after the buffer-resampling fix, and it is the class of bug Papers cannot have because it renders with poppler.

Approach to evaluate, as an optional path:
- Fork the pieces we depend on into https://github.com/orgs/tuxbooks/repositories: chromium/pdfium (the C++ renderer) and embedpdf/pdfium (the WASM wrapper and build), plus whatever build tooling we need to produce the wasm.
- Point TuxBooks at those forks and build the PDFium wasm from our fork instead of the published package.
- Fix the PDFium bugs ourselves in the forks, starting with tuxbooks-i2a (tiling-pattern stroke clipped to the fill path), and carry a small, rebaseable patch set.

What to weigh:
- Cost: PDFium is a large C++ codebase on Chromium build tooling. A maintained fork means we build the wasm on our cadence, track upstream security fixes, and own the supply-chain story (docs/SUPPLY_CHAIN.md, docs/BUILD.md).
- Benefit: we can fix renderer bugs poppler/gs do not have, and stop waiting on upstream releases for them.
- Alternatives: report upstream and wait; accept the leak; or a narrower fork that carries only our patches, rebased on upstream.

Acceptance. Decide whether to fork at all. If we proceed, stand up the two fork repos, produce a pinned reproducible PDFium wasm build wired into TuxBooks, and land a first patch that removes the tuxbooks-i2a leak, verified by the pdftoppm and ghostscript pixel comparison on the plot fixture.
acceptance_criteria: A written decision (fork or not) with the build, security-update, and supply-chain implications; if forked, the two repos exist under the tuxbooks org, TuxBooks builds against them reproducibly, and the tuxbooks-i2a leak is fixed and verified.

comments.author: Tuomo Tuunanen
comments.text:
Forks created under the tuxbooks org:

- https://github.com/tuxbooks/pdfium - fork of chromium/pdfium (the C++ renderer), default branch main.
- https://github.com/tuxbooks/runtime - fork of embedpdf/runtime (EmbedPDF's PDFium fork with the EPDF_* extensions and the wasm build), default branch embedpdf/main.

Correction to the issue text: the npm package @embedpdf/pdfium does not come from a repo named embedpdf/pdfium. Its repository field points at embedpdf/embed-pdf-viewer, directory packages/pdfium (the JS loader), and the wasm it ships is built from embedpdf/runtime. So the two forks above are the ones to patch and build; if we also need to change the JS loader, fork embedpdf/embed-pdf-viewer as a third.

Next: reproduce the tuxbooks-i2a leak against tuxbooks/runtime, build the wasm from the fork (Chromium and emscripten tooling), point TuxBooks at that wasm, then patch the tiling-pattern clip and verify with the pdftoppm and ghostscript comparison.

comments.author: Tuomo Tuunanen
comments.text:
Local setup for the wasm build on Kubuntu 26.04

The fork's CI uses the Chromium toolchain, so this is depot_tools plus emsdk over a short apt list. Nothing here needs more than the release workflow installs.

apt packages:

    sudo apt update
    sudo apt install -y git curl cmake g++ pkg-config tar python3 python3-venv python3-pip xz-utils unzip file

Optional, only if needed: clang and lld for the source tests; ninja-build and lsb-release for a native build. build-target.sh runs build/install-build-deps.sh for non-wasm targets, and that script installs the long Chromium library list itself, so do not hand-install those.

Not from apt:

- depot_tools, which supplies gn, ninja and gclient:

      git clone https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/tools/depot_tools.git ~/depot_tools

  then put ~/depot_tools on PATH.

- emsdk, pinned at 3.1.72 in the fork's release workflow:

      git clone https://github.com/emscripten-core/emsdk.git third_party/emsdk
      third_party/emsdk/emsdk install 3.1.72
      third_party/emsdk/emsdk activate 3.1.72

  then put third_party/emsdk/upstream/emscripten and third_party/emsdk/upstream/bin on PATH.

Then, from a workspace that contains the cloned fork directory:

    scripts/embedpdf-runtime/sync-deps.sh        # writes .gclient and runs gclient sync
    scripts/embedpdf-runtime/build-target.sh wasm32
    scripts/embedpdf-runtime/package-target.sh wasm32

Budget disk and time: gclient sync pulls the Chromium build config, llvm-build and third_party, which is tens of GB, and the wasm build is a long compile. Keep it outside the TuxBooks checkout.

title: PDFium leaks tiling-pattern hatch past the fill path
description:
At high zoom on dphi_GRANIITTI_MC.pdf (Matplotlib plots), PDFium draws the gray hatched error bands slightly past their fill path: short gray flecks/line segments leak about half a line width outside the band edge at the top of each step. Rendering the same page at 614 dpi and comparing: poppler (GNOME Papers/Okular) and ghostscript both have 0 stray ink, PDFium has ~700 pixels of ink where neither reference draws anything.

It is upstream: no FPDF_RENDER_* flag changes it (tested 0x01,0x02,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x200,0x400), the clipped matrix render path (FPDF_RenderPageBitmapWithMatrix) leaks identically, and @embedpdf/pdfium 2.15.1 behaves like 2.15.0. A separate defect found in the same investigation, the full-page buffer landing a pixel short of the CSS box and forcing whole-canvas resampling, is fixed in PdfPageCanvas/pdfiumEngine (buffer is the rounded CSS box times the ratio). This issue tracks only the pattern leak.

Options: watch for a PDFium fix and bump the wasm; or report upstream to chromium/pdfium with the fixture and a poppler/gs comparison. Repro: render page 1 at -r 614 and diff against pdftoppm/gs.
acceptance_criteria: Decide whether to pursue upstream, pin an engine version that clips correctly, or accept the leak; if accepted, document it next to the render budgets.

title: Cap PDF region renders by device scale only for pages with shadings (ADR 0004 option B)
description:
ADR 0004 (docs/adr/0004-pdf-region-render-budget.md) took option A: cap the region render ratio by the whole-page budget for every page, which is safe but softens deep-zoom text on all PDFs. Option B is the preferred refinement: cap only pages that actually contain a shading, so text-only PDFs keep sharp region rendering at deep zoom.

PDFium sizes internal buffers for page-sized objects (a shading's pattern) by the render's device scale over the object's full page box, not by the clip. A large clip at device scale ~43 allocates 380-430MB in one render; the 2GB WASM heap never shrinks, so the high-water ratchets until every render fails with 'Cannot enlarge memory'.

Implementation: add pageHasShading(page) to PdfiumEngine by iterating the page's objects (FPDFPage_CountObjects -> FPDFPage_GetObject -> FPDFPageObj_GetType == FPDF_PAGEOBJ_SHADING), cache the answer per page, expose it beside pageSize through the worker and adapter, thread it to PdfPageCanvas, and use regionRenderRatioForPage only when hasShading is true (plain regionRenderRatio otherwise).

Caveat: detection is coarse (a shading anywhere caps the whole page). If that is not good enough, ADR 0004 option C tiles the region render below the safe clip page area (~21 page units at device scale 43) to keep full resolution for any content at the cost of several PDFium calls per region.
acceptance_criteria: A shaded page (dphi_GRANIITTI_MC.pdf) stays safe at deep zoom and a text-only PDF renders its region at device resolution at deep zoom; pdfRenderPolicy/PdfPageCanvas tests cover the hasShading branch; worker heap stays bounded on the plot zoom-in/zoom-out repro.

title: Align axis-locked wheel scrolling with Evince's dominant-axis rule
description:
Our useAxisLockedWheel (frontend/src/components/reader/useAxisLockedWheel.ts) locks the scroll axis for a whole 300ms gesture and leaves the matching axis to the browser. GNOME Document Viewer instead picks the dominant axis per event: in libview/ev-view.c ev_view_scroll_event it zeroes the smaller of delta_x/delta_y (GTK issue #866), so both axes never move at once, and it lets GTK do the scrolling. Evince's Shift+wheel perpendicular remap is disabled under GTK4 (#if 0), so there is no upstream reference for that path.

Suspected rough edges in our version:
- Shift+wheel horizontal scroll depends on Chromium converting a shifted vertical wheel into deltaX; if a platform reports the shifted event as deltaY with shiftKey, the locked-x branch can scroll by zero.
- A mid-gesture axis flip redirects using event.deltaY even when the locked axis is x, so a trackpad event with deltaX only would not move the view.
- The 300ms quiet window means an intended axis change within a gesture is ignored, which may feel sticky next to Evince.

Not the cause of the PDF zoom view-jump (fixed separately); filed for a later, unrelated pass.
acceptance_criteria: Decide and document the rule (per-event dominant axis vs gesture lock); add a unit test driving delta_x/delta_y combinations, including Shift+wheel, and confirm horizontal scrolling while zoomed in.

comments.author: Tuomo Tuunanen
comments.text: Upstream reference corrected: the GNOME viewer is Papers (github.com/gnome/papers), the Evince fork, which is what the TuxBooks PDF engine was ported from. Relevant source: libview/pps-view.c. Ctrl+wheel zoom is scroll_to_zoom_cb; page-flip-on-scroll is page_scroll_cb (continuous mode returns PROPAGATE, so GTK scrolls natively). The Evince per-event axis zeroing (its issue #866) is inside an #if 0 GTK4 TODO, so Papers has no explicit axis lock either. That means our 300ms gesture lock and the Shift+wheel remap are TuxBooks-only, with no upstream behaviour to match, so the rough edges filed here are ours to define.
